source.title: Minor interpretability exploration #3: Extending superposition to different activation functions (loss landscape)

record.tranche_reason: The post says it re-ran the TMS results using the original code and changed the activation function, reporting superposition results across activation settings.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative outcomes for superposition and its development. It gives no numeric results in the supplied text; linked notebooks, graphs, and tables are not included here. Its discussion of possible causes is speculation, not a tested result.
record.test_reason: The post re-runs the Timaeus TMS autoencoder notebook with many activation functions in place of ReLU. It reports qualitatively how much superposition forms under each, so its results bear on whether V1 holds beyond ReLU. This is a new setting for the same toy method, not a pure replication. All evidence is qualitative text; graphs and tables are only on a linked drive.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The author concludes that more superposition yields marginally smaller losses, and that superposition develops after the initial large loss drop during phase changes. Sharp, non-negative, asymmetric activations gave the most superposition and lowest losses. The author adds that small activation changes cause large superposition differences without matching loss-landscape differences, and calls the sigmoid and SoLU results confusing.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses the TMS notebook and original code, changing the activation functions. It presents this as an exploratory extension across activation functions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported degree and timing of superposition vary across activation functions; the post specifically notes contrasting outcomes for GELU versus ReLU, SoLU versus softmax, and bounded-output functions.

fits_no_version.finding: Superposition emerged only after the largest loss drops and coincided with small loss drops and LLC rises, apparently in flat basins.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TMS training, superposition forms after the main loss drop and coincides with LLC-marked phase changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Beyond a threshold, degree of superposition was not correlated with loss or LLC. Large activation-driven differences in superposition did not show up in the loss landscape.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Degree of superposition in TMS is largely decoupled from final loss and LLC across activation functions.

record.problems: The supplied post gives qualitative outcomes without numerical results, model sizes, feature counts, dimensionalities, or quantitative uncertainty. It describes itself as a small exploration without prior predictions and says several outcomes are confusing. No controls are reported in the text.

untested.parts: Feature sparsity is not varied, so the sparsity-dependent transition is untested. Feature-to-dimension ratios are not stated. Near-orthogonality and regular geometry are not quantified beyond a mention of antipodal pairs for bounded activations.

missing.what: Hard variants of sigmoidal activations reduce or slow superposition. Swish and hardswish show no clear difference.
missing.locator: Results, Specific ("Hardness reduces..."; swish vs hardswish in GELU-group discussion)

missing.what: Low degrees of superposition usually coincide with slower formation.
Bounded-output activations contradict prior reports of significant superposition for Sigmoid (Lad and Kostolansky 2023; project #2).

record.verdict_notes: This is an exploratory LessWrong post with no numbers, controls, or uncertainty in the text. All rows are qualitative impressions, presumably from weight-geometry plots on a linked drive. Tranche changed from T1 to T3 because the contribution is varying the activation function, a new setting. The 'none' for r1 and r12 reflects that loss, LLC and training timing are outside V1's wording.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not state the number of features relative to dimensions or test feature sparsity, a sparsity-dependent transition, near-orthogonal directions, or regular geometry.
